title: Why this one is a ghost
lede: The company is gone. The name has had four owners since 2015 and still sells electronics.

items.title: The stores
items.text: General Wireless, a Standard General affiliate, bought 1,743 stores, many co-branded with Sprint. The rest were liquidated.[^16][^21]

items.title: Mexico
items.text: The Mexican subsidiaries went to Office Depot de México for $31.9M.[^16]

items.title: Second bankruptcy
items.text: General Wireless filed for Chapter 11 and began closing hundreds of stores. Sprint later paid $12M in a settlement.[^26][^27]

items.title: The brand, online
items.text: Retail Ecommerce Ventures bought the brands, websites and the “You’ve got questions” trademark.[^28][^29]

items.title: The crypto detour
items.text: REV turned radioshack.com into a waitlist for a cryptocurrency project, warning visitors about impostor accounts.[^32][^33]

items.title: The new owner
items.text: Unicomer Group of El Salvador, a RadioShack franchisee in Latin America and the Caribbean, bought the IP in about 70 countries. RadioShack-branded stores today are dealer or franchise locations, and the brand sells online.[^30][^31][^33]

blocks.title: Who has owned the name
blocks.subtitle: Three corporate eras before the bankruptcy, and three owners in the eight years after it.

nodes.what: Theodore and Milton Deutschmann open a radio-parts store in Boston, according to the brand’s 2020 owner.[^28]
Charles Tandy’s Fort Worth company buys the struggling chain and makes it profitable within two years.[^18]
Tandy, by then a single chain, takes the name of its stores.[^5][^18]
The hedge fund’s affiliate buys 1,743 stores, many co-branded with Sprint. The rest are liquidated.[^16][^21]
General Wireless files and begins closing hundreds of stores.[^26][^27]
Buys the brands, the websites and the “You’ve got questions” trademark, and in 2022 uses the name for a cryptocurrency project.[^28][^29][^32]
The Salvadoran retailer, a RadioShack franchisee, buys the IP in about 70 countries.[^30][^31]
